newsitem.title: USA: U.S spot propane prices up as Kansas goes haywire.
newsitem.headline: U.S spot propane prices up as Kansas goes haywire.

text.p: U.S. spot propane prices were rising out of their holiday slumber Thursday as prices in the key midcontinent hub at Conway, Kansas displayed the most noteworthy fireworks yet in the new year, traders said.

The volatile price movement at Conway made the market wait all the more intently for weekly stocks data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), which showed at drop of 500,000 barrels to 41.5 million.
Prompt Conway propane prices were notionally pegged at between 69.50 and 72 cents a gallon, after trading variously through the day at anywhere from 64 to 75 cents a gallon.
Traders noted some of the price action -- about 4.00 cents higher than on Tuesday as of late day, was a post-holiday bounce related to the presence of more buyers in the market.

At the same time however, some traders cautioned that while action is again picking up, liquidity remains just light enough to get away with creating rather noteworthy price swings of more than 10 cents in one day.

Other factors, such as talk of TET partially lifting its propane allocation program helped lift prices across the board. Propane in Mount Belvieu, Texas gained 3.00 cents with talk in the 52 to 53 cents a gallon range.
Traders said TET lifted allocations in parts of Ohio, which could stoke buying as far away as Texas.

But other traders warned that supplies appear to be plentiful around the Mount Belvieu hub, and shipping continues to be tight, which means Texas players still cannot get a piece of the European propane spike, and that prices at the U.S. Gulf Coast could thus remain under downward pressure.
On the data front, EIA reported modest drops on the East and Gulf Coasts and said Midwest inventories were unchanged.
The data said East Coast stocks dropped by 100,000 barrels to 4.6 million, Gulf Coast stocks fell by 300,000 barrels to 22.8 million and Midwest stocks stood unchanged at 12.7 million barrels.
-- Oliver Ludwig New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
